Stephen Miller Is a Problem

But only a few GOP senators will admit it.

Joe Perticone

READ TO ME

Good afternoon and welcome to Press Pass, The Bulwark’s twice-weekly newsletter on Congress, campaigns, and the way Washington works behind the scenes. Writing this newsletter involves a lot of idling in the hallways of the Capitol while waiting for an opportunity to press a passing lawmaker on what’s important and where things are heading. You might be surprised at how long I sometimes have to wait and watch before a member of Congress steps into my view. Committing hours to the hunt for stories and quotations is possible only because our Bulwark+ members believe in our independent media outlet enough to support us. I invite you to consider joining them by upgrading to Bulwark+. See what you think of the extras and exclusives that go along with paying membership.

Join now

Today’s edition is packed. First off, a little news about the House Republicans’ choice for their next leader, just announced this afternoon. Then we look at with the selection of Stephen Miller to be Trump’s new White House chief of staff, a move that has some Republicans worried that the president has drawn no lessons from his party’s shellacking in last week’s midterms. Other GOP lawmakers appear to be in denial about what’s going on. I’m sure it will all work out for them in the end.

In addition, to learn how the Democratic majority might function in the new year, I wanted the perspective of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus to see what kind of role, if any, they stand to play in the next Congress’s agenda. Unfortunately for them, last week’s elections have thrown the caucus into disarray. Lastly, what is one of the most experienced legislators in recent American history doing sitting through freshman Senate orientation? Well, having a laugh about it, at least. All that and more, below.

(Photo illustration by Bill Kuchman/The Bulwark | Photos: Getty, Shutterstock)

Run this town

As I was finishing this newsletter, word came from House Republicans that they settled on Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio to be their new leader as they move into the minority in January. With Speaker Mike Johnson saying he didn’t want the job, the choice came down to Jordan, the in-your-face chairman of the Judiciary Committee and Freedom Caucus cofounder, and the widely liked and relatively milder-mannered Steve Scalise, who has spent nearly four years as majority leader after about a decade as the Republican whip. Jordan and Scalise previously faced off in 2023, clashing over who would succeed Speaker Kevin McCarthy; ultimately, neither had enough support, and the job went instead to Johnson.

I just shot a quick video on this:

Empire state of mind

Donald Trump’s decision last week to name Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff gives the impression that instead of learning from and correcting the policy mistakes of the past two years, the president intends to double down on them. Miller has been unapologetically racist, and his prejudices and hatreds have fueled much of the Trump administration’s nativist agenda, especially in the area of immigration enforcement. He will now hold even more power over the administration’s policy direction.

Naturally I wanted to ask Republican senators, newly returned to Capitol Hill on their first day back in session, for their thoughts on Miller’s promotion.

First, I sought out two of the Republicans leaving Congress at the end of the term. I hoped they would offer some unvarnished honesty, and they did not disappoint.

“I think it’s the worst possible thing that could have happened this week,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) told me. “Look, this guy was deputy White House chief of staff and senior policy advisor and homeland security advisor. Tell me, what in Homeland Security before Markwayne Mullin got there was going well for this administration?”

“So, for a year, this guy is helping advise on homeland security where we lost the immigration reform and border security issue, right? And then you take a look at some of the missteps with Greenland and a number of other things,” Tillis added. “[Miller is] the last person who should be trying to settle things down.”

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) was only slightly more circumspect. When I asked him whether last week’s election results, a Republican calamity, warranted some reflection on the past two years of GOP policy—with Miller a leading voice developing it—Cornyn jokingly pointed at Tim Scott (R-S.C.) and said, “I’m gonna talk to the expert here and find out.” Scott, the National Republican Senatorial Committee chairman, has received a drubbing over the party’s extraordinary losses in the upper chamber.

Get Press Pass in your inbox every Tuesday and Thursday

Join

What sort of White House will Miller manage? Based on the man’s character, rhetorical habits, and political priorities, it’s reasonable to assume he will lead in a combative and unapologetic direction, and in ways that may even surpass the already belligerent stance of the first two years of Trump’s second term. Miller has called critics of Trump’s tariffs “economically illiterate, historically illiterate, and probably functionally illiterate.” He has encouraged Fox News to fire its pollster, who showed that Trump’s tariffs were unpopular—and he did so during an appearance on Fox News. He has said Republicans should ignore the “panicans” who were worried about the Iran war. He has called Democrats the “jihad party.” And he called one senator’s criticisms of ICE’s brutality “unimaginably stupid,” all while proclaiming that the world is governed only by power.

Encouraged by the departing lawmakers’ honesty about Miller’s appointment, I also asked Republicans whose Senate careers are still in the safe category if they were comfortable with the man Trump was placing at the wheel. The answers they gave me varied: Some seemed to be in denial, some refused to see the appointment as their concern, and others defended Miller’s character and record, even to a point of outright sycophancy.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), who just secured another six years in the Senate, told me bluntly, “The president decides who he wants as his chief of staff, and he does not ask us for permission.”

Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.) coauthored a bipartisan immigration reform bill in 2024 that Miller harshly condemned as a secret vehicle for “amnesty”; Lankford’s Republican colleagues ultimately tanked the legislation at Trump’s urging. Even so, the senior senator from Oklahoma dismissed the idea that Miller’s xenophobia presents a full picture of his personality and policy priorities, telling me, “Stephen is smart and tough, and he has the trust of the president.”

“I think people should sit down and talk to him,” Lankford added. “Quite frankly, I find a lot of people unwilling to actually have a conversation with him. And people that can sit down and have a conversation with him will find a very different person.”

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), who’s made a name for himself as an unshakeable Trump loyalist, said Miller’s appointment is a signal that the administration is ready for war.

“It is definitely a period of reflection,” Moreno said. “We got our asses kicked. There’s no question about that, and there’s no candy-coating that. None of us should try to dance around that very fact.”

“The president appointing Stephen Miller is pretty straightforward. It’s I think what Senator [John] Thune said today, which is if Democrats want to actually advance an affordability agenda and actually get things going for the American people and help the lives of working Americans and grow our middle class, I think Republicans are all in to help that,” Moreno added. “And if they wanna be idiots and put some of these crazy, socialist mantras in place and go back to Biden-era ridiculousness, then we need to go into the arena like gladiators. And that’s where Stephen Miller comes in.”

Miller has steadily climbed the Trump ladder over the past decade while many of his fellow travelers have fallen into the political abyss from positions several rungs above him. His influence with the president has grown to a point that he has successfully pushed for multiple policies that have directly damaged the economy and sent Trump’s approval ratings through the floor. He’s now in a better position than ever to keep pushing.

Share

99 problems

About a decade after it was founded, the Problem Solvers Caucus is on life support. The bipartisan centrist group’s Republican members suffered such devastating losses in the midterm elections that it is not clear how it will continue to function in the next Congress without a heavy recruiting push.

Prior to the elections, the group’s roster boasted 43 members, with roughly equal proportions of Republicans and Democrats. After the once-in-a-generation Democratic wave crashed across the country last week, a dozen of the caucus’s Republican members have lost or are on track to lose when the final totals are announced. That means that just seven Republicans in the Problem Solvers Caucus will retain their seats in the 120th Congress, compared to nineteen Democrats.¹ (Democratic exits from the caucus were purely the result of retirements; each Democratic caucus member who ran for re-election won.)

“There’s churn on both sides, but certainly a lot more churn on the Republican side right now,” problem-solving Rep. Josh Harder (D-Calif.) told me Monday evening. “But as you know, in a divided government, there’s always members that are willing to work together, and I think there’s especially going to be an incentive for folks that are currently—or going to be—in the minority to find opportunities to build some bridges.”

Unfortunately, the Problem Solvers will not be in a position to solve any problems until they figure out how to make up their losses heading into the new year. Any path forward for the caucus will need to include both a recruitment drive and a new strategic vision for how they might actually influence the House agenda.

Harder noted, “I think there’s going to be a good recruiting push for sure on Problem Solvers and for those of us on [the Build America Caucus],² as well.”

“Time will tell, but I think we have to reconstitute,” Rep. Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.) told me. “A number of Republicans have to see the Problem Solvers as having value—as something that they wanna participate with and commit to because the mission of the Problem Solvers is something that they have to understand and commit to.”

“Certainly, I think there’s hope,” the Democratic problem-solver added. “It’s just a matter of reconstituting and seeing how it plays out.”

“That’s kind of the way that works, right?” said Rep. Blake Moore (R-Utah), one of the few Republicans in the caucus to survive the midterm elections with his career intact. “I mean, when the Dems lose the majority, they lose members of that committee, as well. It’s not unexpected.”

Moore sounded a bit more defeated than his Democratic counterparts in the group, hinting that there will be little enthusiasm for their work from the GOP side.

The Problem Solvers Caucus took its current form in 2017, growing out of earlier negotiations and organizing by the centrist organization No Labels.³ The caucus gains power to help steer the congressional agenda when partisan squabbling reaches critical levels, especially in the context of small margins between the majority and minority parties. But when House Democrats assume power in January, the size of their majority—they will have something like eighty-five more seats than Republicans—means they will have few incentives to reach across the aisle to join hands with their diminished and defeated opponents, whether problem solvers or not.

Leave a comment

Young forever

On Monday, Senator-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) celebrated his 74th birthday. He spent the day in freshman orientation alongside the several other Democrats who triumphed in last Tuesday’s wave elections.

Brown was a bit out of place during these proceedings. He has either run for public office or held it during every election cycle since 1974, when Gerald Ford was in office. That’s a fifty-two-year career in politics, almost two decades of which he has spent as a senator. Perhaps the facilitators threw in some special tips and tricks to help enliven his orientation for the familiar role.

I found the whole situation very amusing. I even posted that Brown must be feeling a bit like Billy Madison:

When I caught up with the new-old senator later in the day on Monday, he told me that people kept sending him my post. As for what it’s like to be the big kid in class, Brown joked, “It’s kinda cool.”

I have included in the Republican tally a likely (but still uncalled) win by caucus member Maria Salazar (R-Fla.); she was leading at the time of writing.

The Build America Caucus is a newer group with a similar orientation to that of the Problem Solvers; it is also composed of centrist members of both parties. The midterm elections resulted in cuts to its Republican side, too.

No Labels is best known for its controversial and ultimately abortive campaign to recruit and run a third-party candidate for president in the 2024 election.

Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend

Where does answer engine optimization (AEO) end and agent experience begin? Inside Resend, from the docs that help Claude Code pick an email API to the tools it uses to send. ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌

Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend

Where does answer engine optimization (AEO) end and agent experience begin? Inside Resend, from the docs that help Claude Code pick an email API to the tools it uses to send.

Read online

Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare.

So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player?

Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025, on the pod today:

Why Coding Agents Keep Picking Resend — Zeno Rocha, Resend

In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models.

Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday.

The developer gets there before the model

Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email

Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. Add .md to the URL and the agent gets a table it can read in one request. That’s the kind of change I liked in our Supabase interview too. You can ask whether a model has heard of your product. You can also open your own pricing table and see whether it can answer a customer’s question.

80 tools, or two?

When we recorded, Resend’s MCP server had grown from roughly 20 tools or fewer at launch to more than 80. Zeno wants someone working in a chat client to be able to do what they can do in the dashboard. Sending an email gets the demo working. Inviting a teammate, checking usage and managing billing account for some of the long tail. The design looks especially interesting alongside Cloudflare’s Code Mode server, which exposes its API through two tools, search() and execute().

Zeno describes opening the collapsed tool calls in his own sessions to see what the agent actually did. In one, the result was too large to fit in context. Reducing the tool count wouldn’t by itself make that response any smaller. For someone designing an MCP server, that’s a cheap experiment worth borrowing: expand the result of a call you make every day and see how much of it the model actually needs.

What happens after “send”?

Getting an agent to pick the SDK still leaves the entire business of delivering the mail. Take click tracking. A provider can rewrite links through a shared tracking domain so it can count clicks. If one customer uses that domain for phishing and it gets blocklisted, links in another customer’s perfectly legitimate emails can suffer too. Zeno explains why Resend introduced custom tracking domains and why he wants to keep the free tier even though spammers can sign up for it. Custom tracking domains · Resend’s $3M safety commitment

Watch the domain setup and pricing walkthroughs if you build developer tools. Stay for the last stretch if you know Zeno from Dracula. We get into what it’s like to build a company with a family and how much of a founder’s job comes down to finding a name that other people actually use.

Show notes

Zeno’s original Dracula announcement — the editor theme he launched in 2013.

Zeno on what Claude Code chooses — his reading of the recommendation study and the differences between model versions.

Resend’s MCP server — the integration behind the tool-count discussion.

Anthropic on writing tools for agents — concrete approaches to returning less data when a tool result fills the context window.

Resend’s anti-abuse handbook — what happens when a new sender signs up and where the team intervenes.

NaiveAI Promises 2,100 Tokens per Second. How Well Does It Code?

NaiveAI could potentially top Artificial Analysis’s speed rankings. Our hands-on test suggests its coding quality holds up against DeepSeek. ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌

NaiveAI Promises 2,100 Tokens per Second. How Well Does It Code?

NaiveAI could potentially top Artificial Analysis’s speed rankings. Our hands-on test suggests its coding quality holds up against DeepSeek.

Gabriele Beltramo | November 10, 2026

Read online

Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space.

Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible. It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI, with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster.

The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5, which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal.

To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention.

NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog, this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate.

Benchmarking NaiveAI vs. DeepSeek and Z.ai

We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive-N0.5-Flash against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash, and then gave all three the same app-building prompts.

The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. However, that comes at a slightly higher cost per question — although that may be an acceptable price for applications where speed comes first.

Most popular models on OpenRouter as of the end of October 2026.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash are two of the most popular models in OpenRouter. Both belong to the Flash model class and demonstrate excellent capabilities in AI-assisted coding.

As of this writing, performance statistics for NaiveAI models are not yet available on Artificial Analysis. Therefore, we report the Intelligence Index scores of the models used in our comparison:

Model Intelligence Index

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max): 45

GLM-5.3-Flash: 43

Naive-N0.5-Flash: not yet available

Published benchmark results offer some insight into the new model's capabilities. They place its coding ability between the two comparison models, and ahead of both on NL2Repo-Bench.

The table below shows benchmark scores reported in the official model cards and technical blog posts of the respective models. Sources: GLM-5.3-Flash – Technical Blog, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 – Model Card, Naive AI – Research.

Model

NL2Repo-Bench

DeepSWE v1.1

Agent's Last Exam (ALE)

Our own evaluations below look at the differences between these models in more detail.

Speed and verbosity experiments

Speed is the headline feature.1 NaiveAI promises faster research iteration than comparable models, which matters to developers and AI researchers who need to test ideas quickly.2

We evaluated each model on 10 randomly sampled, text-only questions at each of three difficulty levels: 10 easy questions from MATH-500, 10 medium questions from GPQA-Diamond and 10 hard questions from HLE-Diamond. That makes 30 questions per model. All experiments used the same maximum completion-token limit of 256K.

For each request, we recorded response speed (tokens per second, TPS), the total number of completion tokens, and end-to-end response time. The code for the experiments is at https://github.com/gbeltramo/llm-verbosity.

The tables below report the mean and median across all 30 successful requests for each configuration. Throughput figures come from different sources: OpenRouter for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash, and server-side measurements for Naive-N0.5-Flash. They should be compared with that in mind.

Graphic by Gabriele Beltramo

Key observations

Naive-N0.5-Flash reports exceptionally high throughput, approaching or passing 1,000 tokens per second in both thinking configurations. Because its figures are server-side and the other models' figures come from OpenRouter, we do not claim an exact speed multiple over DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 or GLM 5.3 Flash.

Thinking has a large effect on verbosity. On the hard HLE questions, Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking on averaged about 108,500 completion tokens, roughly nine times the GLM 5.3 Flash (high) average and 11 times the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) average.

The medians tell a different story from the means. Across all 30 questions, the median completion for Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking on was about 3,200 tokens, far below its average of more than 51,000. A small number of requests produced exceptionally long reasoning traces and pulled the average up. The same pattern appears, less sharply, in the other models.

The tables also include end-to-end response time, which is the fairer basis for judging speed. The median question took 3.1 seconds with Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking), against 5.3 seconds for GLM 5.3 Flash (high) and 10.1 seconds for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high). The means are closer: 45.3 seconds for Naive-N0.5-Flash, 45.0 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, and 86.9 for GLM 5.3 Flash. On the hard questions, Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) was slower on average than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high), at 89.8 seconds against 79.7.

Two caveats apply. The sample is small, at 10 questions per difficulty level, and we did not grade answer accuracy. Short, fast replies are only useful if they are correct.

App experiments

We also asked the models to build the same web apps from the same initial prompt. We tested six combinations of model and thinking effort, with the thinking effort in parentheses:

Naive-N0.5-Flash (no thinking)

Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking)

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (low)

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high)

GLM 5.3 Flash (low)

GLM 5.3 Flash (high)

The gallery of apps is available online. In summary, the three prompts asked the six model variants to do the following:

Create an interactive 3D view of the Earth and the Solar System.

Grow a 3D tree from a seeded random generator, with branches that taper and fork, thousands of leaves, and bark and leaf textures.

Do a browser port of the book Ray Tracing in One Weekend.

Below we’ve embedded results for the thinking variants of each model.

Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking)

Earth and the Solar System; Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking)

3D tree; Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking)

Ray Tracing in One Weekend; Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking)

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high)

Earth and the Solar System; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high)

3D tree; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high)

Ray Tracing in One Weekend; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high)

GLM 5.3 Flash (high)

Earth and the Solar System; GLM 5.3 Flash (high)

3D tree; GLM 5.3 Flash (high)

Ray Tracing in One Weekend; GLM 5.3 Flash (high)

Solar system

The first app is an interactive 3D view of the Earth and the Solar System. Viewers can orbit the camera around the scene and watch the planets circle the sun, with controls to speed up or slow down their motion. Every surface is drawn from generated textures, with no image files.

Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) produced the best result of the three. Its sun shows sunspots, and the dark side of its Earth glows with city lights at night.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) came close behind. Its version lacks an asteroid belt, and its Earth has less textural detail.

GLM 5.3 Flash (high) stumbled on lighting, which makes the planets hard to tell apart. Its speed controls are also too sensitive, so a small nudge sends the planets racing or crawling.

Tree modeling

The second app grows a 3D tree from a seeded random generator, with branches that taper and fork, thousands of leaves, and bark and leaf textures. Wind makes the branches sway and the leaves flutter, and the shadows on the grassy ground move with them. The tree stands under a sky gradient and light fog. A control panel adjusts the seed, branching depth, leaf count, wind strength and direction, and sun position. There’s also a switch to autumn colors and a frame-rate counter sits in the corner.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) and Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) both produced good results. The surprise was Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking switched off, which did not produce a usable app at all.

The good results still had small glitches in the wind animation. In the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) app, thin branches can detach from their parents in strong wind and appear to float. The effect is subtle, but it is there.

The problem is easier to see in the GLM 5.3 Flash (high) app. When the wind intensity is turned up, the whole tree starts to deform and wobble like a jelly sculpture in an earthquake.

Ray Tracing in One Weekend

The third app is a browser port of the book Ray Tracing in One Weekend. It renders the book's cover scene: a vast gray ground, a scatter of small matte, metallic and glass spheres, and three large spheres in the center. One is glass, one a brown matte and one a polished metal. Depth of field blurs the foreground and background. The image builds up progressively on screen, with a progress bar, elapsed time and a rays-per-second estimate. A menu offers the book's earlier milestone scenes. The user can pick a quality preset and download the result as a PNG.

In this more coding-focused scenario, all three models with thinking on produced a working app.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) wins because its ray tracer is the most efficient of the three. It also uses the full width of the screen to display the rendered image.

The Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) app is correct, but its JavaScript is less efficient.

GLM 5.3 Flash (high) is again the weakest. Its speed is similar to the Naive-N0.5-Flash app, but its interface is more basic.

Pricing

Naive positions N0.5-Flash as a capable, low-cost model. The target prices are $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.40 per million output tokens, and $0.01 per million cache-read tokens.

That puts it in the $0.20 to $0.60 per million output tokens band occupied by several capable Flash models, including the two we compared it against.

The final bill will also depend on how many tokens the model uses. That in turn depends on the thinking budget requested and the difficulty of the questions.

Takeaways

In ultrafast mode, Naive-N0.5-Flash can peak at around 2,000 tokens per second and sustain nearly 1,000 during thinking-heavy tasks.

In our tests, its median response time was several times shorter than those of GLM 5.3 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 at their high thinking settings. Mean times were similar to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017.

On complex tasks, it spent far more thinking tokens than the other two models. On easy and medium questions, it consistently replied faster.

In the apps, Naive-N0.5-Flash was much more consistent than GLM 5.3 Flash (high). With thinking on, it also holds its own against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. It built the most detailed solar system app, tied with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 on the tree model, and came a close second on the efficiency of the ray tracer.

For developers who value fast iteration over token economy, that speed is the main reason to try Naive-N0.5-Flash.

1 The speed of Naive-N0.5-Flash depends on an efficient speculative-decoding drafter and a custom inference engine. The reported decoding speeds were measured on a single eight-GPU Blackwell node running speculative decoding in NaiveRT. The drafter was Naive-N0.5-Flash-FP8-Draft, and the setup is tuned for single-stream decode latency rather than batch throughput.

Realized speed depends on how many draft tokens the target model accepts per round. That varies with the checkpoint pair, the prompt, context length, sampling settings, and the content being generated. The reported numbers show this clearly:

- Acceptance rate: 70.6% with thinking disabled, but only 43.4% with thinking enabled.

- Decode speed: about 984 tokens/s in the thinking phase and 1,816 tokens/s in the answer phase.

- Peak rate: roughly 2,100 tokens/s over a single second. Treat this as an upper bound, not a typical rate.

The engine matters as much as the drafter. The developers report that a full speculative round (draft, verify, sampling and commit) takes 3.4 ms in NaiveRT versus 12.3 ms in SGLang, a 72.4% reduction. The thinking-disabled campaign measured about 3.45 ms per round. For the full measurements, see NaiveRT: Performance.

2 Implications for reinforcement learning: Generating autoregressive rollouts is the main bottleneck in large-scale reinforcement learning. Anything that cuts decode cost, such as the sparse attention (DSA) adopted here, makes rollouts cheaper. Adapting other models to DSA could make that loop considerably more efficient and speed up frontier research.

This fits Naive AI's larger promise: a self-improving AI that can optimize its own inference CUDA kernels and adopt the most efficient architecture for large-scale reinforcement learning training.

Can Nigeria’s 2027 Election Deliver Hope?

As Nigeria prepares for the 2027 national elections, campaign season is already underway. After the promise of “change” in 2015 and “renewed hope” in 2023, Nigerians are weighing persistent frustrations over the cost of living, insecurity, and concerns about the credibility of the electoral process, at a time when democracy itself is under strain across West Africa.

In this episode of Into Africa, Oge Onubogu is joined by Professor Jibrin Ibrahim, Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Centre for Democracy and Development - West Africa (CDD-West Africa), a distinguished Nigerian political scientist and democracy advocate with more than three decades of experience across academia and civil society. Together, they explore what Nigeria’s security and economic challenges reveal about the state of its democracy, the relationship between citizens and the state, and what is at stake as the country heads toward 2027.

The Download

The billionaire tax that wasn’t

Morning Brew Inc.

TL;DR: What do tech billionaires, construction workers, and a Democratic governor have in common? They were all against California’s billionaire tax, and they won. Last week, voters rejected Prop 40, a one-time 5% levy on the state’s richest residents that looked simple on paper—in the first big test of a wealth tax, right on tech’s home turf.

What happened: The tax would’ve applied to anyone worth at least $1 billion who lived in California at the start of the year (about 200 to 300 people), and tech would’ve footed much of the bill. Unlike most taxes, it was targeted at wealth instead of income, which matters because most billionaires’ fortunes are tied up in stock (for reference, Mark Zuckerberg’s base salary at Meta is $1).

On paper: A healthcare workers union pitched the measure as a way to make up for federal cuts that are expected to leave about 2 million Californians without health insurance. Supporters say the tax would’ve generated about $100 billion in revenue for the state, with 90% slated for a healthcare fund and the rest for education and food assistance. As the AI boom sent billionaire fortunes soaring, supporters argued, they could easily afford a one-time hit.

Reality check: So how does a tax on a few hundred billionaires lose in California? For one, the people campaigning against it had a far larger war chest and outspent its supporters roughly tenfold ($378 million to $32 million). Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the charge with more than $100 million alone and was joined by fellow tech heavyweights, including Eric Schmidt and Peter Thiel.

The logic against the tax is a tale as old as time: If billionaires leave (which many threatened to do if the tax went into effect), the companies they founded and the jobs they create could go with them. When Zuckerberg floated leaving, Meta created a whole new class of shares he could sell to cover the tax (most of us can’t even expense lunch). And the argument won over an unlikely coalition, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, construction unions, and the state’s largest teachers union. Others objected to how the measure was written, arguing there was no guarantee the money would boost healthcare or help in other areas.

Bottom line: There could be a rematch in 2028, but it now faces a new hurdle: Prop 42, a countermeasure that would ban new state taxes on assets like stocks and business stakes—which is on track to pass. Tech companies can, for now, cancel their U-Hauls and go back to building robots to drive them. —LC

This 1 iPhone setting can expose your nosiest app

Ever wonder what your apps are up to when you’re not looking? Turns out, your iPhone can tell you. The App Privacy Report, buried in your phone’s settings, shows you which apps access your location, camera, microphone, and contacts, and which web domains they connect to.

How to turn it on: Open the Settings app → Privacy & Security → App Privacy Report → Turn on App Privacy Report. It’ll only include activity from after you turn it on and show the seven most recent days.

The report can be overwhelming at first glance (here’s what it looks like), so focus on these two things:

Data & Sensor Access: Tap an app to see exactly when it used your camera, mic, or location. (For example, it makes sense for a rideshare app to check your location. It might not for a crossword app.)

App Network Activity: Look for telltale words—domains with “ads,” “analytics,” “metrics,” or “measurement” in the name usually point to tracking services.

Spot something you don’t like? Go to Settings → Privacy & Security. Choose what you want to restrict (like Location Services, etc.) and switch off access for any app that doesn’t need it. —LC

The Zeitbyte

Space gets DOOMed

A segment of DOOM gameplay the satellite captured on board frame by frame. Tanagra Space

The human race has reached one very important milestone: playing a 1993 video game in space. Recently, a group of amateur Norwegian radio operators managed to launch the classic first-person shooter Doom on a satellite orbiting hundreds of miles above the planet. And they did it in much the same way you’d tell Alexa to play your favorite album—by speaking a voice command to the satellite.

This might be the first time earthlings have sent orders to a satellite via voice command, per Tanagra Space, a firm that develops AI software for spacecraft and helped organize the experiment. But it’s definitely not the first time people have gotten Doom running on an unconventional platform. Gamers have ported it to: a John Deere tractor, a pregnancy test, a graphing calculator powered by roughly 100 pounds of rotting potatoes, and even on E. coli cells. While the demonstration doesn’t show whether anyone actually beat a Doom level on the spacecraft (you can see the “postcard” it sent to Earth here), we’ll mark this down as one small code execution for a satellite, one giant launch for satellitekind. —WK

Snapshot of the day

November 9, 2026

Sidharth Bhatia, Anirudh S.K.

As expected, the BJP-led Mahayuti’s candidate has won the election to the post of chairperson of Maharashtra’s influential Gokul Dairy. That’s not because of the strength of his candidature but because the Devendra Fadnavis government brazenly tilted the playing field in favour of his side by allowing government-nominated and designated directors to vote in the chair’s election days after the Congress-led bloc trumped the Mahayuti in the main board election. Former Nationalist Congress Party MLA Rajesh Patil’s victory today comes just a day after Congress leader Satej Patil led a massive protest in Kolhapur – where Gokul is based – that was attended by thousands of people.

Though Fadnavis has sought to justify his move in the lead-up to the chair’s election by saying that the lack of a quorum had forced his hand – lest the board election itself be nullified – Kunal Purohit points out that there was no quorum on October 29 because Mahayuti directors had abstained from the meeting that day.

The US federal court for the southern district of New York has allowed Khalistani separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun – who Washington alleges was the target of an assassination plot orchestrated by former Indian intelligence officer Vikash Yadav – to serve summons on national security adviser Ajit Doval and former Research and Analysis Wing chief Samant Goel through Indian courts. This is in connection with a civil lawsuit that Pannun, a dual citizen of America and Canada, filed two years ago naming the Indian government, Doval, Goel, Yadav and Nikhil Gupta, whom the US government has accused of trying to execute the plot allegedly orchestrated by Yadav. Pannun’s lawyers have said they previously tried to serve the summons to Doval, Goel and Yadav through the Ministry of Law and Justice in New Delhi. Separately, the US state department confirmed that it transmitted the summons and complaint to the Indian embassy in D.C. last month.

On Raisina Hill, the external affairs ministry rejected that there is any path to serving summonses in India that bypasses the law ministry. “We reject the fabricated and malicious attacks on our high officials. As also we reject the frivolous lawsuits,” ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal also said.

Three workers at Tata Electronics’ iPhone manufacturing hub in Hosur, Tamil Nadu died in the line of work yesterday night; they had inhaled gas while inspecting a filtration facility at one of the effluent treatment plants at the site. The incident marks the latest setback for Apple’s India ambitions – it makes about a quarter of all iPhones here as part of its bid to diversify production away from China – and Tata, which was hit by a cyberattack earlier this year.

Because they travelled for official programmes or to be with their families, many Union ministers on Diwali escaped having to be in Delhi, which has the dubious distinction of being one of the world’s most polluted capital cities round this time of year. For instance Prime Minister Narendra Modi was in verdant Bastar, defence minister Rajnath Singh was in alpine Sikkim and parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju was well clear of Delhi’s noxious air in Riyadh...

NEWSLETTER · 10 Nov 2026, 18:02

The trilateral no one’s talking about

Also, in tonight’s edition: EU and US close ranks behind NATO ahead of Abu Dhabi

VIEW IN BROWSER

By Eddy Wax

With Magnus Lund Nielsen

Hello, and welcome to Rapporteur PM.

Trilateral meetings are all the rage this week.

Manfred Weber, Iratxe García, and Valérie Hayer, the leaders of the European Parliament’s centrist political groups, will meet at 08:15 on Wednesday to officially kick off talks on the midterms.

Don’t expect any US-style waves. Despite the American terminology, there is no new public vote, meaning the same political dynamics will govern the talks. The only changes – if there are any – will be a reshuffle of parliamentary positions and prestigious posts. The headline question is who should hold the presidency, a role currently held by Roberta Metsola.

The Socialists, led by García, and Renew, led by Hayer, are demanding that Weber’s European People’s Party publicly endorse a written coalition agreement committing to refrain from further voting alliances with Eurosceptic conservatives, nationalists or the far right.

Weber has not yet publicly endorsed such an arrangement but is keen to secure another term for Metsola, who could become the longest-serving European Parliament president if she remains in post until 2029.

His European People’s Party (EPP), already the dominant force in the Parliament, wants things to stay as they are and has warned the socialists (S&D) that they should be happy to keep their five allotted vice-presidents, especially given how things are looking for Pedro Sánchez in Spain.

García is keeping her threat to field a candidate against Metsola in reserve, making a written policy agreement with the EPP a priority.

The mood among the centrist groups is not as bad as it has been.

Recent agreements between the EPP and S&D to share rapporteurships – for instance, on banning children’s access to social media and an affordable housing legislation – have calmed tensions somewhat.

But still, the talks expected to run until the plenary votes in January, could go south.

The EPP has been voting with the so-called Venezuela majority – spanning the Eurosceptic conservatives to the far-right ESN group, home to Alternative for Germany. It is unlikely that Weber will want to tie himself to the S&D and the liberals on too many topics.

After Abu Dhabi, there’s no shortage of trilateral meetings that won’t change the course of European history.

Round-up

UNITED FOR NATO: After much back and forth, the Americans and Europeans have closed ranks in support of NATO with a statement published before talks began in Abu Dhabi. “[A] strong NATO will remain central to Euro-Atlantic collective defence,” representatives wrote.

TRACTOR, BUCKLE UP: EU farmers are staging a rally when European leaders meet in Dublin later this week. Farmers plan to plough “No CAP cuts” into fields near the airport to catch the eye of leaders flying into the summit. CAP is shorthand for the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy.

MERZ VS MAGYAR: Hungarian PM Péter Magyar clashed with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin on Tuesday over proposals to link the EU's increasingly fraught budget negotiations to continued financial support for Ukraine. Leaders in both Czechia and Slovakia have accused Merz of blackmail.

DON’T EAT THAT: French experts suspect that an increasing reliance on AI to identity mushrooms has led to an uptick in poisoning cases. In October, 211 people suffered mushroom poisoning, compared with 74 in the same month last year.

10 November, 2026

Martha Henriques

Earth editor

Hello. As the world's largest producer of greenhouse gases, China's shift towards renewables has the potential to influence global emissions more than any other nation. Extensive efforts to clean up its energy production have brought the country close to achieving a major milestone: plateauing its emissions. In today's Future Earth, Xiaoying You outlines five ways China achieved the feat. Plus: why the world's most expensive spice is disappearing.

CLIMATE CONVERSATION

How China is leading the climate charge

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTYsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAABxf7Oc_8igaQSDzV0d_69rlH8TUMIdR_ap56Gc-fVuKO-ViESTuoleHlAYLQUCBiD_iQYZSNvWbNsQzkwY8Bkc7Ja0yS43SSJiL8u5wv China now has five times more solar and wind capacity than the US. Credit: Getty Images

For a country as large as China, it will be difficult to know precisely when emissions are really declining.

Independent analyses now show the growth of China's annual greenhouse gas and CO2 emissions has dramatically slowed in recent years, and some experts believe China has already passed its emissions peak - five years ahead of its own deadline.

Whenever the precise peak happens, the changes now being seen in China mark a significant step for the climate, given the country's overall contribution to global emissions.

THE BIG PICTURE

Why the world's most expensive spice is disappearing

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTYsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAABxf7OdABYcKxSEthzCYWjKtwraXGXbf4VhmlHC3pLpKCGucuXmA2F6okkbZwn1Ov98mvuglDkM-T7zPA-ns0WCdRNqOnDlZyVeVe1px4 Roughly 4,000 flowers are needed to produce just one ounce (28g) of saffron. Credit: Getty Images

Saffron is one of Kashmir's most treasured exports, with its high price on the global market earning it the nickname "red gold".

While the vast majority of the spice is produced by Iran, the saffron from Kashmir is particularly revered for its unique flavour and aroma. It plays a vital role in Kashmiri culture, used in everything from tea to traditional medicine and perfumes.

However, climate change poses an existential threat to Kashmiri saffron growers, who are already seeing the devastating impact of sustained warmer, drier weather on their harvests.

Expert Q&A

Abhinav Subramaniam

Abhinav Subramaniam is a research associate for the Energy Security and Climate Change Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. In this capacity, Abhinav manages program budgets, coordinates project activities, and delivers administrative and research support for initiatives across energy, technology, and sustainability. Abhinav holds a B.S. in mechanical engineering from the University of California, Berkeley.

Read full bio →

Q: What are the key differences between the U.S. and Indian power systems?

There are several clear differences between the two countries: India operates on a national unified grid, where the U.S. has a fractured regional structure with varying levels of federal oversight.

Most U.S. utilities are privately owned with select public entities – this mix is reversed in India, where most distribution utilities are publicly owned, with only select private utilities in predominantly urban areas.

Q: How does transmission infrastructure contribute to U.S. energy security, particularly in strengthening grid reliability, resilience, and the flexibility of the power system?

Transmission across stakeholders is recognized as the ultimate way to build reliability, support demand growth from data centers, electrification, and reindustrialization, and reducing rates long-term. Building transmission, especially long-range and interregional transmission is especially critical to improve geographic resource diversification, improving regional coordination, and taking the burden off expensive and less reliable local transmission lines.

As the U.S. invests in novel energy sources like geothermal, nuclear, long-duration energy storage, the siting of power will become a greater constraint. Building reliable long-range transmission can make these projects more bankable and improve efforts to further indigenize America's energy mix.

How I got seduced

It took them 5 years

Ben Tossell

Nov 10

READ IN APP

Is it just me or does everyone else see Ramp sponsoring everything under the sun?

Over the past few years it’s like I’ve been brainwashed to think more and more about Ramp. They sponsor my dreams. Rumour has it if you say ‘Ramp’ three times in a mirror, an accountant appears.

To be honest, I don’t even fully know what Ramp is or does - receipts? a bank? developer tool? or a marketing stunt company?

So I did some research to see how they infiltrated my brain.

I turned it into a very visual, interactive page that I encourage you to look at. It’s just not the same in the email :(

Ben’s Bites is brought to you by Adobe

Adobe Firefly, the AI creative studio, lets you describe what you want to create, then review the Adobe Creative Agent’s plan before it gets to work using Creative Cloud tools.

You stay in control from first idea to finished result. Try it today in the Firefly Assistant!

Just look at that chart above. It’s crazy (1) how accurately it’s drawn and (2) how the closely related the trend of revenue, valuation, and how much they’re in my eyes and ears over time is.

But their product isn’t ‘sexy’.

If we look at the next super accurate chart of how hard companies have to try vs how boring their product is, we can see how Ramp and others move from the expected baseline.

They get it. They have the illustrious ‘taste’ factor. They have fun with it.

For example, who’s the world’s most famous accountant?

Kevin from The Office (US) of course. So they did the only reasonable thing they could. Stick him in a glass box in New York and have him process 600k expense reports.

200+ Million people saw this stunt. A couple even got married in the box...wtf!?

They also recognise that the ‘exhaust’ from these efforts turn into great content too. In these receipts sections (on the live post) you can click to see the real videos and images.

Then they doubled down on Kevin (Brian), or more accurately 10x’d him by sending 9 lookalikes with him to the Super Bowl. Plus also hosted a Brian-themed party in SF where people came dressed as him with a lookalike competition where the winners got Super Bowl tickets. They sold bald caps called ‘Brian Hair’ too - reminds me of the Pitbull bald-cap mania.

Oh and of course he was in the ad itself.

A year before the Brians, they made their first Super Bowl ad in a week.

I’ve been diving into Colossus magazine recently, they do awesome in-depth profiles of people and companies. Well worth reading. But outside of the awesome profiles I actually saw awesome display ads.

I’ve never said ‘awesome display ads’ in my life, and doubt anyone else has either. But these ads were made (assuming with the help of AI) to be super personalised and unique to the content of the post itself.

These were my favourite:

They came in like a wrecking ball 🎶 to launch Ramp Treasury.

To launch bill pay, they put on a Broadway musical.

Last month, they got Tony Hawk on a ramp outside the NYSE.

These stunts make noise for a wide audience but they understand their customers deeply. Not just CFOs/Controllers but founders and developers.

They sponsor a lot of podcasts. This is where I think they’ve entered my brain more often than I’m comfortable admitting.

They also turn up in odd places. I’ve heard of “test new ad channels before other companies get there” but I’ve never seen an ad in a church bulletin before.

Last Christmas, they put Claude Code in RollerCoaster Tycoon.

They built their own coding agent, Inspect. Which they used internally for a while before opening it up for others to use.

And a model router.

And Glass, a knowledge platform for teams.

There are so many areas where I may become a Ramp customer that is not their core offering. But it feels like Amazon starting with books, seeing what other people want to buy and adding that too.

They build with AI tools, they track spend, they ship tools to help their team move faster, more efficiently and spend less. All of their customers want that too, so why not productise it. And land some new customers in the process.

How do they do it all? Eric, the CEO, talks about empathy and then taste as two values for Ramp. Another mentions velocity as a key component of their culture.

They switched up how they do marketing, what products they build for customers and also how the organisation works.

And the stunts come from a team of seven.

If we layer everything onto the super-accurate chart we started with, it’s interesting to see how velocity, taste and experimentation really helped accelerate growth for Ramp.

But more interestingly it’s all after a down-round in valuation where usually all the weird things are cut away in favour of doing what ‘normal’ companies should do.

And that may be why Ramp is doing so well...

Ramp don’t sponsor me (maybe they should?!) but I’ve just been floored by how much fun they seem to be having. Their whole strategy for the last few years is so smart. To me it’s truly tasteful in how they’re doing what they’re doing, how they understand the game of attention, and how to reach the customers they want - in and out of their peripheral ‘TAM’.

Weekly Graphic: Making Sense of Hormuz Traffic Data

Today's Updates from Geopolitical Futures

Weekly Graphic: Making Sense of Hormuz Traffic Data

By: Geopolitical Futures - November 6, 2026

Ships are returning to the Strait of Hormuz, but oil is not. Nearly 770 vessels crossed the strait in October, close to July’s wartime peak of 795, yet the oil they carried out fell to an estimated 39.5 million barrels, roughly a quarter of July’s 151.3 million, according to transponder data from the Strait of Hormuz Ship Monitor. The gap reflects Iran’s campaign against tankers on the southern route near Oman, which Tehran deems illegal; Iranian forces said at least five tankers were damaged by mines and fires on Nov. 5 alone, while the U.S. blockade keeps Iran’s own crude out of the count.

The true volume is likely higher, since many tankers now sail with their transponders switched off, and commercial trackers using satellite imagery report substantially larger flows. Gulf producers have also found ways around the chokepoint, with Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq and Kuwait exporting a combined 15.5 million barrels per day in October, roughly prewar levels, according to Bloomberg, aided by a 35 percent jump in Saudi shipments from the Red Sea Port of Yanbu and the UAE’s pipeline to Fujairah.

Tehran, meanwhile, is turning access into leverage: An Iranian lawmaker said ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar are exempt from its restrictions, and Iran has offered to reopen the strait within two days if Washington meets its terms. Markets remain on edge, with Brent plunging more than 7 percent on Nov. 2 on hopes of a deal before rebounding on reports of U.S. strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island. Any agreement will ultimately be judged by whether it brings tankers, not just ships, back through Hormuz.

Headlines & Launches

Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 (12 minute read)

Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, featuring improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, with up to 30% faster output generation and lower pricing. The models share the same underlying architecture.

Google's New TPU Lineup (4 minute read)

Google introduced TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and higher compute density, alongside TPU 8tx for secure and confidential inference.

Introducing Meta Ember (3 minute read)

Meta introduced Muse Ember, a small reasoning model optimized for agent tasks such as tool calling, coding, and document parsing. Meta claims it matches Claude Haiku 5.5's highest reasoning score at roughly one-third the cost and outperforms GPT-6 Luna across reasoning settings.

Deep Dives & Analysis

AI R&D Is Accelerating Towards Potential RSI in 2027 (62 minute read)

AI is accelerating AI R&D at Anthropic. The company is now estimated to be several months ahead of the AI 2027 timeline. We may be less than a year away from full RSI, and there are no clear bottlenecks in the way. We now need to prepare for scenarios where critical events happen in 2027 or 2028.

When Does the US Become a Net Importer of Tokens? (3 minute read)

The US could become a net importer of AI tokens between 2028 and 2030. Domestic capacity can accommodate roughly 2.5x annual token growth, with faster demand growth or canceled data center projects pushing computation overseas.

Will Anthropic Grow Into Its Compute Bill? (13 minute read)

Anthropic needs an estimated roughly $200 billion in annual revenue to support its average compute commitments through 2030 at current spending ratios. Its $895 billion commitment total exposes it to demand shortfalls, margin compression, delivery delays, and expensive short-term capacity when demand exceeds forecasts.

🧑‍💻

Engineering & Research

LiveKit 101: build a humanlike voice agent in under an hour, in your browser (Sponsor)

Want to build a voice agent using the same tech used at OpenAI, SpaceX, and NVIDIA? Join a 60-minute virtual workshop with LiveKit's Solutions Architecture team, where you'll build your own voice agent in the browser and talk to it before the session ends. Join live and build together.

Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)

Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)

Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

NVIDIA Introduces Hardware-Aware LLM Compression (24 minute read)

NVIDIA's AutoCompress framework optimizes LLM pruning for hardware-specific latency, throughput, and memory constraints rather than parameter counts alone. It compressed Nemotron 3.5 Super from 120B to 74B parameters while retaining its performance.

Miscellaneous

Anthropic Buys $3.4 Billion in Gas Generators (2 minute read)

Anthropic reportedly secured 1.7 gigawatts of Caterpillar gas generators for $3.4 billion, taking over equipment orders from supplier OnePWR. The purchase moves the AI lab deeper into physical infrastructure as power shortages and lengthy grid connection queues constrain data center expansion.

Apple Introduces $50 AI Usage Packs in Logic Pro (2 minute read)

Apple now sells $49.99 Intelligence Usage Packs in Logic Pro to extend access to cloud-based AI features after users reach their limits. Unused capacity rolls over monthly but expires after 12 months, and purchases cannot be shared through Family Sharing.

Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI

The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity

Sponsored by MIT Sloan Global Programs

Claim 50% off + bonus AI reports

By Thomas Macaulay • 11.10.26

Hello!

Today: Nancy Pelosi’s successor tells us how he hopes to slow down AI before it gets out of control. Plus: Why the backlash to the US data center buildout may be less about politics than the electricity they consume.

Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI

—Grace Huckins

As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times.

“We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI. Here’s what he plans to do about it.

The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity

—James O’Donnell

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash sweeping the country arguably first began to take shape.

Big Tech has framed the data center uproar as a culture war over progress. But a few days in Ashburn convinced me the real fault line may be electricity: drawing it from the grid or generating it onsite provokes different forms of blowback.

The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Find out why.

The Spy Who Leased Me

Emergency pod with Chris McGuire on l'affaire Jensen

͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­͏ ­
