The Spy Who Leased Me

Emergency pod with Chris McGuire on l'affaire Jensen

Jordan Schneider

Nov 10

READ IN APP

On Sunday, Jensen Huang emailed all of Nvidia to admit an affair, and his board opened an investigation into whether the woman, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, was working for China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed, the Singapore cloud company suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China, is still buying them.

To make sense of it we have Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and Emerging Technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former NSC Deputy Senior Director for Technology and National Security.

We discuss…

The May 2025 decision that made Megaspeed possible — Commerce stopped enforcing the Biden-era license rule for big chip orders to third countries, never replaced it, and $80 billion in AI chips went to Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand this year alone

Why the spy matters more than the affair — Jensen talks chip policy with the president, knows who has what compute, and decides who gets it next

The defensive briefing nobody gave — why not warning Jensen was a choice rather than an oversight, and how Commerce sat on the intelligence while $4.8 billion in chips shipped

Corruption or incompetence — Cantor Fitzgerald’s Nvidia position, an under secretary who never explains the policy, and a Commerce investigation discussed with the target’s main business partner

What the lame duck can fix — MATCH, RASA, and OVERWATCH, plus the smuggling and remote-access loopholes only Commerce can close

A brief history of honey traps — Jael’s tent peg, Cold War Romeos, and the compromised officer who got parked at the Hoover Institution

Listen now on your favorite podcast app.

Emergency Pod: L’Affaire Jensen

Jordan Schneider: I think we should workshop some titles for this episode. I’ve got Lust, Compliance by Ang Lee. The Spy Who Leased Me. Hopper, Blackwell, Rubin, Spy. Crouching Tiger, Hidden Asset. Where are we going with this?

Chris McGuire: I like The Spy Who Leased Me. Maybe I’m a little biased on the James Bond front.

Jordan Schneider: Emergency podcast: L’Affaire Jensen. Here we are, Monday, November 9th. We’ve gone from “close relationship” to “romantic relationship” to “by the way, I got the feds off the hunt of my girlfriend’s company that’s smuggling chips,” question mark.

I’m old enough to remember January of 2025, when this administration came in talking a big game on China. I remember Lutnick saying something like, “They’re disrespecting us by trying to steal our chips, and we’re not going to stand for it.” For the first few months, it seemed like the policy you worked on in the Biden administration was by and large going to continue: chips are important, and China shouldn’t be able to get whatever chips it wants. Then all of a sudden Jensen Huang comes into the picture. Pick it up from there, Chris.

Chris McGuire: Jensen has repeatedly lobbied the government to loosen export controls. There’s been so much focus on loosening controls on chips to China, but where I think he’s had even more impact is preventing the enforcement of controls on third countries that China is using to get access to chips.

There’s a lot of debate about H200s and whether we should send chips to China — obviously, I think no. But the more consequential decisions happened in May 2025, when the Trump administration decided not to enforce the Biden administration rules that would have prevented exports to Megaspeed. The Biden administration said any large AI chip orders to non-trusted companies in most countries in the world are going to require an export license. The Trump administration said, we’re not going to enforce that. They also said they were going to replace it, and then they never did. The regulations that are still on the books would have prevented this situation. But the Trump administration made the decision, at the request of Jensen, not to enforce them.

Since then, you’ve seen a gradual whittling down of export control policy and a blurring of the lines. It’s no longer a clear, definitive “the US will not allow China to access the most advanced chips.” It’s, well, certain ones they can, certain ones they can’t. There are loopholes. They’re enforcing this, they’re not enforcing that. It’s created a hodgepodge where, first, it’s not even clear what export control policy is at this point — you can’t understand it when you go look at the regulations. Second, it’s created massive gaps that China is exploiting to gain access to chips, particularly via Southeast Asia.

That seems like what was happening with Megaspeed. On top of this, you’re now seeing that there were inappropriate relationships between the leadership of Megaspeed and the leadership of Nvidia, and all sorts of other stories adding on. But the core issue is that the restrictions designed to prevent Chinese circumvention of controls — designed to prevent companies like Megaspeed from existing — are not being enforced. That’s why we’re in the situation we’re in today.

Why It Matters That She’s a Spy

Jordan Schneider: For all the Nvidia bulls on Twitter: why is it bad that Jensen Huang slept with a Chinese spy?

Chris McGuire: To be clear, the problem is that she’s a Chinese spy. There are separate stories about infidelity that I don’t think anyone really cares about here.

Nvidia is an extremely strategically important company. They make one of the most important products in the world, which is why they’re regulated by the US government. And Jensen Huang has a personal relationship with the president of the United States. He talks with him about AI policy, chip policy, export control policy. That’s all extremely valuable information to the Chinese, and it’s information we really have to protect.

Not only that, he has all sorts of insight into Nvidia. He knows the details of their chip design. He knows who has what compute — Nvidia knows more about who has how many AI chips than anyone else in the world, far more than the US government knows. And Nvidia is the decider of who gets the compute. Because there’s so much more demand than supply, Jensen is the arbiter of who gets things when. Access to Jensen means access to more compute.

Was that exploited by Megaspeed in order to get compute? I don’t know. Maybe. But if I were the Chinese, that would certainly be an avenue I’d want to pursue to get as many of the most advanced chips as possible, especially given they can’t just buy them normally.

The Briefing That Never Happened

Jordan Schneider: I feel bad for the wife. I feel bad for the kids. I’m not sure I feel bad for all the Nvidia employees who must have been involved in facilitating this — he’s a scheduled enough person that you can’t carry on affairs without your people knowing.

Do I feel bad for President Trump? Not at all. My impression is it was a boys’ club, Epstein, “this will be our little secret” thing, and that’s why he didn’t necessarily get the briefing. Maybe there’s a generous reading where they’re up on him and up on her and it’s part of a broader investigation, but it doesn’t really smell like that to me.

Chris McGuire: On the defensive briefing question, I don’t know the answer, and none of us do. What I would say is that in these situations, the fact that there was not a defensive briefing given is a choice, and one that was probably considered.

Exactly what the reasons were, I don’t know. There are frequently decisions made on that front by the people running this. Like you said, is there a separate investigation into the US person? Maybe it’s just to preserve sources and methods, because they don’t want to lose the access they have on the foreign person. Maybe it’s something else entirely.

Jordan Schneider: Sources and methods, though? People stop having affairs all the time. Your first thought isn’t necessarily, “Oh, the government told the guy I’m sleeping with that I’m a spy.” You could finesse that a little bit, I would hope.

Chris McGuire: Potentially. It depends on what other information they’re getting from Megaspeed. This probably wasn’t just useful on the Jensen front — this is obviously an entity the US government is tracking. There are a bunch of possible reasons, and we can’t really speculate as to why they didn’t. But the fact that he didn’t get a defensive briefing is probably a choice, and not just “oh, people forgot to do this.”

Where does this all go from here? There are going to be a lot of difficult questions inside Nvidia. They’re going to have to do their own internal investigation, and people can generally leave that to them.

The big question for Congress and for the administration is how the Commerce Department could have known that Megaspeed was being run by Chinese spies and not done anything to stop the export of chips to them. $4.8 billion worth of chips, and they were sitting on information that said the company is being run by Chinese spies, and those spies are actively trying to penetrate Nvidia at the highest levels. It’s baffling to me how they could have sat on that and done nothing. That warrants questions in the administration and congressional oversight. There are obvious steps Commerce should take right now to mitigate this, but why did they sit on it for a year and not do anything?

Jordan, if you have any ideas for what a reasonable explanation is, I would love to know. I can’t even come up with one.

Corruption, Incompetence, or Cantor Fitzgerald?

Jordan Schneider: There’s going to be a lot of Democratic activity around corruption. And there’s corruption that’s gross, like the Binance stuff, and then there’s corruption that harms the national interest and sways grand strategic things that matter, which is more like all the UAE money.

Jensen is giving money, but he’s not putting it in the pockets of Donald Trump. He’s giving money to the ballroom and to the presidential library, which, granted, is legal. This is different from paying someone’s son-in-law for a pardon. But if you’re a Democratic staffer and you want a corruption story that’s a two-for-one — not just exposing this administration for being gross, but for being negligent in its duty to preserve American national power — I would really think about sinking my teeth into this.

It is baffling. We’ve done so many shows about this over the years, and we were saying yesterday that it doesn’t add up. If you really want to run the playbook of “we’re selling all the chips into China because we think that’s the right thing to do,” then run that playbook and sell all the chips into China. But this half measure — we’re going to say we’re not enforcing the rule, but it’s still on the website, sort of, and then maybe he puts a footnote out…

Maybe it’s not corruption. Maybe it’s incompetence. Maybe it’s the inability to make a decision on something that really deserves one. This is a big strategic call, and the executive branch has a lot of autonomy to make it go or no-go on AI chip controls. And we have Nvidia able to reverse decisions that were seemingly already made, on command, because this guy who’s sleeping with a Chinese spy calls up the president. It’s a juicy one, man. Makes me want to get a law degree. Almost.

Chris McGuire: When we’re talking about motives, I don’t know what it is, but this also highlights the importance of having clear disclosures about where people’s money is, and being confident that people are not finding other ways to get paid.

There’s a lot of talk about Lutnick and Cantor Fitzgerald and the ties there. If you look at Cantor Fitzgerald’s public SEC filings, their third-biggest exposure is to Nvidia stock. It’s also their third-biggest unhedged exposure, behind the S&P 500 and Amazon. And their two bigger exposures in total are AMD and Marvell. So Cantor Fitzgerald is very heavily indexed on semiconductor stocks. Obviously they’re right to be bullish — semiconductors are doing very well. But it’s a very bad look, in the context of adopting policies that are so obviously preferential to an individual company, that Cantor Fitzgerald holds a ton of that stock.

Jordan Schneider: This wasn’t Lutnick, but Witkoff gave the quote at some point in the past two years: “I’m not conflicted. My kids now run my business.”

Chris McGuire: Right. I mean —

Jordan Schneider: There’s not much more to be said.

Chris McGuire: There’s not. We need to have stronger standards on these things.

The Largest Tech Transfer in History

Chris McGuire: This year alone, the number two, four, and five importers of AI chips are Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand. Collectively, they’ve imported $80 billion worth of AI chips just this year. That’s not all necessarily for China, but I’ll bet you a lot of it is. This is a consequence of the policy lapses. Collectively, this has resulted in not just these insane scandals involving the biggest or second-biggest company in the world, but also the largest technology transfer of controlled goods in history between the United States and any of its adversaries.

This is an insane scandal. Why was this allowed to happen? We don’t have any answers. Under Secretary Kessler has given basically zero public remarks in his entire time as BIS under secretary. Other than his testimony to Congress, he hasn’t said anything. Why are we doing this? What is the policy? Someone explain it. Secretary Lutnick, please explain it, and explain the details.

I would love to hear that. In the absence of a good reason, the suspicions about the really malfeasant reasons are only going to grow. That’s problematic for the integrity of the institutions and of export controls. I hope it’s wrong, but the suspicions are only going to go up.

Jordan Schneider: They could explain it, or they could just go away. It’s been two years. Are the next two going to be more fun, guys? It’s way more fun to investigate people who still have the jobs than people who’ve left. So insofar as they don’t want to become poster children for Chinese espionage and corruption, maybe it’s time to head back to private practice, or Cantor Fitzgerald, or what have you. Free career advice from ChinaTalk.

Chris McGuire: Or just change the policy. Fix the policy error that resulted in this. That’s the most important thing that needs to happen, regardless of who does it. It would make some of the noise go away, because you could at least say, “We fixed it.”

Right now, Megaspeed is buying chips. Today. Still. It is still listed on Nvidia’s website as an official cloud partner. That’s shocking to me. I don’t understand how they could have not taken that down.

Jordan Schneider: It’s funny, because Chinese companies are more used to this. When someone writes an article about them spying on Uyghurs or something, it’s usually down within a few hours. Nvidia just isn’t used to being caught up in giant national security scandals, so they don’t quite have the delete function ready on all the contracts. What’s the force majeure in your GPU allocation contract for “your CEO and a spy”?

Chris McGuire: So many things about this are baffling. But this whole situation never added up. The explanations for selling chips to China never added up when you have US companies clamoring for chips. You have Elon Musk and Andy Jassy saying, “We can’t get enough chips, we want more chips,” and meanwhile Nvidia is adamant that we have to sell more chips to China. I still don’t really understand why. One possible explanation is that they’re captured, but I don’t really think so.

The data Nvidia has been putting out about the Chinese threat has always been overinflated, and not consistent with what we’re seeing in Huawei’s actual chip production capabilities. When you look at the numbers, they tell such a different story than the one Nvidia was telling. And now it comes to light that there was a direct relationship between their CEO and a spy. It’s impossible to say exactly why, but this massively hurts their credibility on export control policy and on China policy going forward.

The company will deal with the company’s business. We just have to see the policy changes we need, and we know what those are. Some of them are already on the books. This isn’t an impossible problem. It requires a modicum of political will. A lot of people in the administration already want to do this. Commerce has been singularly obstinate. We’ll see how long that lasts, but I hope the pressure remains bipartisan and ramps up.

From Tribes 2 to the Balance of Power

Jordan Schneider: I always had this idea in the back of my mind that China would be interested in popping the US AI bubble at some point. I thought it would be a rare earth control, maybe on interconnects or packaging. I did not have on my bingo card that a spy gets caught and everyone gets worried about whether Nvidia keeps delivering.

Chris McGuire: To be clear, no one wants that. Jensen has done an incredible job with Nvidia, turning it into the company it is, making the best product in the world, better than anybody else. This doesn’t take away any of that. But the reason the products are controlled is that they’re so good they have significant national security applications. It just doesn’t seem like the company has caught up to the reality of what it’s making and is behaving accordingly.

Jordan Schneider: Cheating on your spouse: not great, not a crime. Advocating for your business, lobbying the White House, wanting to sell your stuff to China — totally within the bounds of what’s reasonable.

The piece that never quite clicked for me is this. This guy was a gaming CEO who made gaming chips for 30 years. Then all of a sudden, what he was making goes from a thing that lets me play Tribes 2 —

Chris McGuire: I remember Tribes 2.

underrated classic

Jordan Schneider: — shout-out Tribes 2 — to a technology of grand strategic importance. And throughout all of it, he kept arguing that on the one hand, these chips are so important that every industry and company in the world needs them and they’re going to revolutionize society, but on the other, they’re not going to revolutionize militaries and they won’t matter for the global balance of power.

It’s a weird argument, but it makes sense if you still have the demeanor and mindset of a technology guy whose work doesn’t really interact with nation-states. Having affairs with your Chinese clients who have connections to foreign intelligence is indicative of him never really internalizing just how important his chips are to the global balance of power.

Chris McGuire: Absolutely. There’s a broader recognition that needs to happen across the tech industry. Banks went through this evolution a long time ago. Sanctions policy is now taken very seriously. There are a lot of internal controls to make sure they do as much as possible to comply, and they generally recognize the importance of the US financial system in the geostrategic environment. The tech community’s not there. The government has recognized the importance of it, but —

Jordan Schneider: They want to have it both ways.

Chris McGuire: Exactly. And other nation-states are actively pursuing them. Don’t just look at Nvidia. Look at the OpenAI situation with the Saudis recently, where it looks like DOJ is alleging that the Saudi government was involved in some kind of plot to spy on OpenAI. I’m not surprised. Of course they would do that. This is a strategically super important technology that just happens to be made in the private sector. Other governments are going to try to acquire it, and they’re going to go to the private sector.

The private sector has to up its game. They have to take national security seriously in their lobbying. They have to have internal security, cybersecurity, and physical security measures. And general compliance, oversight, and governance have to be better.

The US government has to constantly close every single loophole, every single time, because any way Nvidia can squeeze out a sale to China, they’ll do it. Then we have to write a regulation that prevents it, rather than just coming to an understanding of “we don’t want you selling to China.” If you could have that, the whole environment would be so much easier. That’s not the course they’ve pursued, and it’s created this adversarial regulatory environment. Then you see this on top of it. That’s where a lot of the hostility and frustration in Washington comes from. It doesn’t have to be that way. We can have a cooperative relationship on these things, but it requires companies to really understand where the US government is coming from and act accordingly. This just shows we’re not close to that.

What Congress Can and Can’t Fix

Jordan Schneider: Let’s talk fallout. The MATCH Act, RASA [the Remote Access Security Act], OVERWATCH — what do these revelations do for the prospects of these bills in the lame duck session?

Chris McGuire: Undoubtedly this spotlights them and makes them more likely. These are already bipartisan bills, and we’re already seeing bipartisan concern. You had the Republican chairs of the Intelligence, Foreign Relations, and China committees all send letters to Nvidia. You’ve also seen Democrats talking about how they’re going to conduct oversight — Senator Warren is the incoming Banking chair, Senator Coons the incoming SFRC chair.

The NDAA is currently being negotiated and finalized. If the NDAA passes, I imagine those bills will be attached to it. There are some open questions about the status of the NDAA given the elections, and especially Democratic concerns about Iran, the Defense Department, and all sorts of unrelated things.

What would send a really strong message is if Congress just pushed them now. We don’t have to wait for the NDAA. These could go separately — unanimous consent, or individual bills in the Senate and the House. These are bipartisan measures with the support of leadership and the vast majority of the House, at a time when we’re seeing such concern about how these things are being handled. I don’t know if that will happen, but I do think those bills will become law. It’s just a question of when.

But they address some of the problem, not all of it. OVERWATCH makes clear: no Blackwells to China. MATCH will cut off DUV, which is very important, and will force the administration to move generally on SME controls. But you don’t have anything that comprehensively gets at the counter-smuggling problem, the remote access problem, and some of the other loopholes.

So you really need the Commerce Department to take those actions itself. They need to impose license requirements for large-scale AI chip orders globally and for all orders in Southeast Asia. They need to impose restrictions on remote access. They need to ban Chinese companies from buying chips in the United States. The only place in the world where Chinese companies are legally allowed to buy chips is inside the United States of America.

Most of the chips Megaspeed got, it seems, came from a company called Aivres, which is the US subsidiary of Inspur — and Inspur is on the entity list. This is insane. The subsidiary of an entity-listed company is legally buying chips inside the United States.

We need Commerce to tighten all this up and make clear that our policy is the president’s policy. The president’s policy is no Blackwells to China. Make that clear across the board, and make sure there’s no Blackwell access for China anywhere. Right now it’s just so porous.

I hope we see that. But realistically, the track record is extremely poor, and it seems like something is preventing Commerce from taking these actions. If all it took was logic, Commerce would have done this a long time ago. If all it took was a push from others in the government, Commerce would have done this a long time ago. They are isolated and adamant in their position.

Hopefully congressional pressure and oversight add to that and force action, but I don’t know if it’s going to happen in the near term, because this behavior is strange. I still don’t understand how Commerce leadership got information that said Megaspeed is run by Chinese spies, and they did not block chip access. The fact that that’s the case means —

Jordan Schneider: Get them addicted, Chris. Get them addicted.

Chris McGuire: — I can’t possibly say in good faith, “Yeah, I think we’re going to solve this problem in the near future,” because it seems like there’s a systemic issue inside the Commerce Department. I really want someone to explain it to me. Give me some answer that makes some sense.

Jordan Schneider: Kessler, if you want to come on ChinaTalk, we’ll make some room for you in our schedule. Just saying.

Chris McGuire: Tell anyone why. And one other thing. The New York Times had a report today saying that Under Secretary Kessler talked with Nvidia about Commerce’s ongoing investigation into Megaspeed, which is crazy. Imagine the FBI was running an investigation into a company, and FBI leadership talked about that investigation with the CEO of that company’s main business partner. Obviously that would be super, super wrong. That’s exactly what happened here.

Not only that, Nvidia had the gall to say that Megaspeed has definitively been shown not to have any diversion and that all the investigations concluded. No — the Commerce investigation got shut down because DOJ took it over, because they said, “You can’t be trusted with this, because you’re talking with their competitor companies.” Everything that’s happening here is so wrong, so not how we handle policy or legal enforcement issues, and it has crossed so many red lines.

Jordan Schneider: There are many sketchy Trump administration things that have happened which you can kind of understand — if you don’t care about the law, or you want your kids to make some money on the side, or you’re just kind of into Putin or dictators or whatever. But this one has landed in a really odd, mysterious place.

A Brief History of Honey Traps

Jordan Schneider: Are we ready for my historical honey traps segment?

Chris McGuire: I love it. Let’s do it.

Jordan Schneider: I did watch Notorious last night. It was excellent. Cary Grant is just —

Chris McGuire: Always good.

Jordan Schneider: First off, everyone gives Delilah credit for being the OG Bond girl, getting Samson’s secrets out of him. But I want to give a little airtime to Jael. Judges 4: “And he said to her, ‘Stand at the door of my tent, and if any man comes and asks you, “Is anyone here?” just say no.’ But Jael, the wife of Heber, took a tent peg and took a hammer in her hand and went softly to him and drove the peg into his temple till it went down into the ground as he was lying fast asleep from weariness. So he died.”

Look, Delilah got her 1,100 shekels, but she didn’t literally put a peg into someone’s brain. Shout-out to Jael. True killer, true innovator in the biblical honeypot game.

I read this book called Honey Trapped, from 2021. With anyone who writes the history of honeypots, the interest is a little prurient. It’s not top-notch historian writing, but it did make for a fun read.

Chris McGuire: I like that your list includes Casino Royale, which featured a male honey trap. So this is not exclusive to one gender.

Jordan Schneider: They’re called Romeos, Chris. They have their own name. This was a big thing in the Cold War in particular. The idea is you get someone to start sleeping with the secretary and get your secrets that way. There was some really awful gay kompromat. There’s one story from the ‘50s in the UK where they drugged and raped a naval attaché of the Soviets, then used the photos to convince him to hand over secrets for a decade. Not ideal.

I did like that there was one person the CIA found was compromised, but they didn’t want him to be disgruntled, and they weren’t ready to throw him in jail because it wasn’t clear he’d given up any secrets. So they just gave him a job at the Hoover Institution. This is in the 1950s.

Jordan Schneider: For whatever reason, this is not really an American thing. The Israelis have done it. In 1986, a Mossad agent got someone to fall in love with her, then drugged him and smuggled him from Italy back to Israel to face justice, which I found kind of impressive. Should we have this playbook, Chris?

Chris McGuire: I would hope that generally we are availing ourselves of all the opportunities we have to collect critical intelligence. But there are, understandably, some personal boundaries we respect for our intelligence operatives. I don’t know the truth. I don’t know to what degree this is encouraged or discouraged. But look at media and history. Look at The Americans — half the plot is about honey traps. On their side, obviously, not ours.

Jordan Schneider: The Soviet use of this tactic actually goes back to czarist Russia. The Okhrana was very into long-term undercover work. They were the ones who wrote The [Protocols of the] Elders of Zion, to discredit the Jewish Bolsheviks with the bourgeoisie. There’s an excellent book on the history of the Soviet deep-cover program, which lasted until the present day. Even Putin still does this.

Chris McGuire: They found the people in Virginia, what, ten years ago or so.

Jordan Schneider: It’s called The Illegals, by Shaun Walker. It came out in 2025.

Another rather prurient one: apparently, in both Poland and France, there were brothels that expressly had the Nazi officers sleep with the prostitutes who had STDs, to undermine the war machine. Feels like decent revenge.

Chris McGuire: Really, all gloves were off in that conflict.

Jordan Schneider: You think total war is a game?

Chris McGuire: The fact that that was made using Nvidia chips is the ultimate irony of all of this. It’s so great that the technology in question is actually being used. That speaks to the greatness of America. So, thank you.

Although that chart in there — Malaysia, Megaspeed, $2 billion, spy — that’s kind of all you really need to know. Nailed it right there. Why doesn’t anyone show that chart to the Commerce Department?

Big Tech & Startups

Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI (18 minute read)

AI models are likely to soon cross the boundary into Artificial General Intelligence. Claude Fable 5.2 is almost as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks that can be completed with a computer. It still makes mistakes and requires human guidance, but it demonstrates impressive work in many tests. There are still important areas in many tasks where the model is jagged enough to fall well behind human capability, but it isn't about simple errors or hallucinations anymore.

Google Escalates Nvidia Rivalry With Specialized Versions of AI Chips (11 minute read)

Google is rolling out two new variations of its Tensor Processing Units. The 8tx is aimed at handling secure, confidential work for customers like government agencies and companies in regulated industries. The 8i Max is designed to run AI applications that require long-context windows. Google's TPU business has proven to be lucrative, and the company has netted some high-profile clients including Apple, Meta, and Oracle.

Science & Futuristic Technology

New Units of Knowledge (8 minute read)

Difference will become the valuable scarcity when AI becomes the main producer of content. The value will lie in doing things in a way that AI does not. Cheap variation is not the same as valuable difference. What yields scarcity will be a distinction worth paying attention to.

Experimental mRNA therapy promotes repair after heart attack damage (3 minute read)

Researchers have developed a treatment that uses mRNA therapy to reawaken heart muscle cells so that they start to divide and help repair damaged muscle. The treatment helped mice produce stronger heartbeats following a heart attack. While not a full cure for heart disease, even small improvements to heart function have been linked to lower mortality. The treatment is short-lived and localized, and is not expected to cause any permanent modification to the heart cells. Further trials in larger animal models are required before human testing can begin.

Storybook 11 beta (6 minute read)

Storybook is a small, development-only workshop that lives alongside your app. It provides an isolated iframe that renders components without interference from app business logic and context, helping developers focus development on each variation of a component. Storybook 11 beta brings official skills and headless CLI tools that let agents iterate autonomously in a smaller package with faster context delivery.

chrome-capture (GitHub Repo)

Chrome 153+ has a native MP4 tab recorder. chrome-capture records Chrome tabs at 60 to 120 frames per second in up to 2160p straight to an AVI .mp4. The recording includes tab audio. Users can start and stop recording whenever they want. Chromo writes AV1 into the mp4 as it goes.

Miscellaneous

How Product Hunt almost died (14 minute read)

Product Hunt needed an acquisition to survive. Markets can change quickly. Assume each consecutive round will be 10 times harder than the last, and know the risks if you're planning to pitch the growth narrative. It only takes one 'yes', so create a wide funnel and find people you can speak to without the mask. Try to divorce your emotions from the outcome.

Anthropic Prepares to Push Ahead With IPO Despite Market Jitters (4 minute read)

Anthropic plans to start trading its shares by the end of next week. Investors anticipated a target valuation of around $1.5 trillion last week, but some major investors are now pushing for it to be lower. Anthropic could still decide to delay its plans and wait for more favorable conditions, but doing so could spark panic in the market. Even before the recent market volatility, investor enthusiasm had been waning for AI names due to increasing concerns about the increasing investments required and a lack of clarity on their potential payoff.

TOP OF THE AGENDA

What the superpowers' energy contest means for the world

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTYsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAABxS2xv6I4Q8bcu-RveJ1r17sLkh-yk5G6VrBsfW4HO-kVAtR7re1rEt0Rvnq-DO_CsGxRZiclP6Lffd9pPXFepwNQ5W2NDzHER2_gcA The UK is investing in offshore wind to generate clean energy, but is reluctant to work with Chinese firms. Credit: EPA/Shutterstock

As the Iran war continues to fuel a rise in oil and gas prices, two global superpowers are fighting to pursue different energy policies. The US is betting on fossil fuels, while China is focusing on the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace them. For the countries squeezed in between, the path they take - buying gas and oil or going with renewables - will shape not just household bills, but how fast planet-warming emissions can be cut, writes climate editor Justin Rowlatt. The US is not expected to send a delegation to COP31 in Antalya, Turkey. Without US pressure, other countries may not make bold promises - but China is beginning to fill the space.

Russell Brand's ex accuses him of abuse

Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison on Monday after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

BEYOND THE HEADLINES

How Epstein survivor was sent by model agency to his home

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNTYsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAABxS2xv6h74JqRRw-TQ_OC0nfUCxleG7lCkhSgHNwqJWG0HHz-jXn1ylv4m1hHPUDoPKOCDBaBYrg-3zvssq6Vfb1YHuVc5nfv-hQP0I Roza, who had arrived in the US from Uzbekistan just a month before she was sent to Epstein's home, says the agency failed her.

When Roza was 18, her model agency sent her to Jeffrey Epstein's Palm Beach home. It was 2009 and Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work from his residence. Roza says those photoshoots led to her being employed as an assistant to Epstein, who went on to systematically rape her. The president of MC2 Model Management at the time, Jeff Fuller, now runs another US model agency called The Source Models. Fuller has not responded to the BBC's allegations. He has previously said he did not know Roza was being abused.

Hello,

Here are the five things you need to know today:

IRAN. As Trump buys time, his methods get stale.

UKRAINE. RUSSIA. Diplomats gather to go through the motions.

MOLDOVA. Maia Sandu builds a Western lifeline.

CYPRUS. Signs of rapprochement in Nicosia.

CHINA. The Nvidia scandal starts to rot from the head down.

Modelled on the Presidential Daily Brief, Geopolitical Dispatch gives you the intelligence you need in the time you have. Subscribe to read all five analyses.

Upgrade to paid

IRAN. Status TACO

As Trump buys time, his methods get stale.

Iran denied there was any deal on Hormuz after oil prices fell as Trump said the war was "effectively over." Trump urged Congress to "stand up" for Pete Hegseth, "perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the country".

INTELLIGENCE. Tehran denies it proposed to reopen the strait for $8 billion, or meet JD Vance, after Trump spoke with Qatar’s prime minister and said he’d continue the “status quo” despite daily calls from Israel to finish the job. Yet not only is the status quo not working for the US – with the release of another 2.7 million strategic reserve barrels and Monday’s evacuation from RAF Mildenhall – but Mojtaba Khamenei has ordered the IRGC to “resolve” matters.

FOR BUSINESS. By reheating the “Trump Always Chickens Out” trade, the US can massage oil prices lower, but an old TACO will soon be inedible and, at best, will only buy time for Hegseth to survive an impending impeachment motion or Benjamin Netanyahu to negotiate a new coalition. Beyond this, Iran risks winning a battle of attrition. While the blockades are hurting, a non-market economy can survive longer than any dependent on confidence and capital.

UKRAINE. RUSSIA. Kabuki Dhabi

Diplomats gather to go through the motions.

Officials from Kyiv, Moscow, and Washington arrived in Abu Dhabi Tuesday for the first trilateral talks since February as Trump claimed both sides were “tired of fighting.” The EU’s Kaja Kallas said Russia was only “pretending” to negotiate...

Traces of Justice review – ‘Chinese Sherlock Holmes’ at centre of arresting forensic cop thriller

Traces of Justice review – ‘Chinese Sherlock Holmes’ at centre of arresting forensic cop thriller. Based on real scientist Cui Daozhi, this sharp feature has thumping set pieces and knotty puzzles set across 30 years of gripping cases The latest from Chen Sicheng, prime mover behind the hit Detective Chinatown franchise , offers a disarming mix of propaganda, copaganda and gripping narrative. It’s essentially a portmanteau biopic: its hero is Cui Xun, a fictional stand-in for the venerable Cui Daozhi , a still-extant real-life figure who so revolutionised forensic science he became known as “China’s Sherlock Holmes”. Ripping three-and-a-bit tales from the casebook – involving a 1970s child killer, a grisly 1980s multiple murder and a 1990s bus bombing (plus one lingering loose end), Chen constructs a history of forensic investigation that is also, in variably oblique ways, a history of Chinese law enforcement, which is shown evolving from boozy, gloveless crime-scene trampling to something far more streamlined and professional. Within the handsome period framework, Chen follows the science: one era’s crazy innovation becomes commonplace in the next. A rookie Cui (played here by Zhang Yi, ageing up subtly) uses boiled potatoes to take dental imprints; when these run out, he and his colleagues start biting one another’s cheeks to make their points. (Their scars are a terrific visual gag: scientists literally showing their working.) By the 90s, when Cui is heading a team working out of a vast, well-staffed warehouse, we seem mere moments away from David Caruso’s sunglasses and memorable Who guitar riffs. The forbidding subtext is presumably that, after 50 years of such breakthroughs, there’s no more getting away with it; as one suspect insists: “everyone pays for what they’ve done.” Continue reading.

Even Martin Scorsese uses AI for storyboards. Can the art survive?. As Hollywood begins to adopt the technology, the professionals in most direct jeopardy are the illustrators mapping out directors’ first visions. They sketch out what could be lost A film industry dominated by AI is a dystopian prospect: stories and dialogue generated by large language models, populated by reincarnated screen icons and uncanny humanoids That is in the future, but the real-world impact of AI is already directly affecting jobs behind the scenes, as Hollywood’s biggest film-makers begin to adopt the technology. James Cameron – long an advocate for emerging technologies in film-making – is on the board of a gen AI firm , citing his interest in how AI will intersect with CGI; Steven Soderbergh used Meta-powered tech to create animations for his recent documentary about John Lennon ; even Christopher Nolan, while dismissing the idea that AI will replace humans as “nonsense”, conceded that it will create some useful “imaging tools”. The current canary in the coalmine however is the storyboard artist, whose work gen AI appears to have directly in its sights. Storyboard artists are the illustrators who draw the panels of images with notes and diagrams that map out scenes before they are filmed. Storyboards are used to work out how a film will look, and as a blueprint to communicate a director’s vision to cast and crew , and are one of the first steps in bringing a script off the page. Now they appear on the verge of replacement by programmes that use text prompts to create illustrations instead. Even an old-school diehard like Martin Scorsese has got on board; in June he announced a partnership with an AI firm whose text-to-image model he used in the storyboarding process for his next movie. Alice Huang may have had access to Nvidia information, too.
